title: Variable-mass sine-Gordon with point defects: integrability, soliton transmission, and quasi-conservation
authors: A. R. Aguirre, H. Blas, H. F. Callisaya, M. C. de Oliveira
abstract: We study integrable variable-mass sine-Gordon model (vmSG) with point defects. Using the Lax and Bäcklund-gauge formulations, we construct type-I and type-II defect matrices, derive the corresponding sewing conditions, and generate the bulk and defect contributions to an infinite hierarchy of conserved charges. The lowest members reduce to the standard sine-Gordon energy and momentum in the homogeneous limit, while for inhomogeneous backgrounds they define integrability-generated energy- and momentum-type quantities. Defect compatibility imposes matching conditions on the variable-mass functions across the defect. An analytical transmission factor $z$ characterizes soliton transmission, topological conversion, and absorption/emission processes. We then deform the type-I sewing conditions by parameters $α$ and $β$ and derive the associated defect anomalies. Consistent one-soliton transmission is recovered for $αβ=1$, whereas for $αβ\neq 1$ parity-centered kink-kink and kink-antikink transmissions display vanishing lowest order integrated anomalies but no generic vanishing at higher order. Numerical simulations reproduce the integrable transmission/conversion regimes and show that non-integrable defects generate weak radiative tails and lowest order quasi-conserved charges, while quasi-conservation of the higher order charges remains unestablished. These results elucidate how exact defect integrability deforms into charge-dependent quasi-conservation and establish a framework for defect-controlled soliton transport in inhomogeneous media, with potential applications to nonuniform Josephson junctions, magnetic and nonlinear-optical systems, and effective molecular and DNA models.
summary: This paper analyzes the variable-mass sine-Gordon model incorporating point defects to study its conservation laws. Using advanced techniques from integrable systems, the authors show that exact integrability is lost unless specific parameters match, leading to a regime of charge-dependent quasi-conservation. This provides a theoretical framework for understanding soliton transport in inhomogeneous media.
main_problem: The study investigates the integrability, soliton transmission, and quasi-conservation properties of the variable-mass sine-Gordon model when point defects are introduced.
main_result: Exact defect integrability is maintained only when a specific closure condition ($\alpha eta = 1$) is met; otherwise, the system exhibits charge-dependent quasi-conservation.
method: The authors employed Lax and Bäcklund-gauge formulations to derive conserved charges, followed by numerical simulations on a two-half-line geometry to analyze defect-induced anomalies.
model_or_system: The model is the variable-mass sine-Gordon equation with point defects, which is analyzed using techniques from integrable systems theory, including defect matrices and sewing conditions.
key_observables: Conserved charges (Energy, Momentum), the soliton transmission factor ($z$), and defect-localized anomalies.
important_parameters: Deformation parameters $\alpha$ and $ eta$, which control the transition between integrable and non-integrable defect regimes.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the existence of a Lax pair and that outer boundaries are far enough from the defect such that generated signals do not return during the simulation time.
figures_summary: The notes reference figures showing finite-difference results, illustrating the transmission/conversion regimes and the effects of non-integrable defects.
paper_structure: The work progresses from establishing the infinite hierarchy of conserved charges in the standard sine-Gordon model using Lax pairs, to generalizing this to the variable-mass case, and finally introducing deformations ($\alpha,  eta$) and numerical simulations to study the transition to quasi-conservation at defects.
why_interesting: The framework establishes a detailed mechanism for how exact integrability breaks down into controlled quasi-conservation due to defects, which has direct implications for modeling physical systems like Josephson junctions or nonlinear optics.
